Normative cross-language conformance vectors for the 0.7 API of apple-purchase-receipt-verifier (docs/design/0.7-api.md), schema version 2 (fixtures/cases.schema.json).
It replaced the 0.6 file of the same name (schema version 1, in git history before 0.7.0). Every 0.6 case is carried over and none is deleted: legacyId names the 0.6 case each one replaces, and a case without legacyId is new in 0.7 (tag new-in-0-7).
No expectation here was produced by running an implementation. Values were carried from the 0.6 cases or derived from the design, then checked against an independent decode of the fixture bytes written for this file. A vector that disagrees with a port is a bug report against one of the two until a human decides.

Operations. verifyReceipt(base64), verifySignedData(jws) and verifyReceiptEndpoint(environment, requestJson) are the three public 0.7 methods. verifyReceipt: a text fixture is handed over verbatim; a raw or base64 fixture holds DER, which the runner encodes as canonical standard base64 with padding. verifySignedData: the fixture's logical bytes as a string (utf8 trims, text does not). verifyReceiptEndpoint: input.fixture is wrapped by the runner as {"receipt-data":"<string>"}, the string built as for verifyReceipt; input.requestBody names a text fixture that is the whole request body, handed over verbatim. decodeBase64 is the one internal hook: 0.7 exposes no decoder, but a valid-base64 string that is not a receipt fails as MALFORMED through verifyReceipt just as invalid base64 does, so the accept side of the base64 rule is only observable on the decoders themselves. Each port's test code calls its receipt-data decoder and its x5c-entry decoder directly; a refusal is MALFORMED from receipt-data and INVALID_CERTIFICATE from x5c (an error group states MALFORMED and the runner maps it for x5c).

Config. trustedRoots is {"source":"defaults"} for Config.defaults() (the three bundled, pinned Apple roots) or {"source":"fixtures","fixtures":[...]} for roots read from registered trust-anchor fixtures. The endpoint takes environment PRODUCTION or SANDBOX. There is no bundle id, accepted environment set, appAppleId or device id anywhere: 0.7 takes none of them, and the eight 0.6 policy cases now verify and pin the value the caller judges (tag policy-flip).

Clock. When a case carries clock.now the runner builds its Config with a clock fixed at that instant; otherwise the default clock runs. 0.7 reads the clock in two places: the certificate-validity instant when the input states no usable date (a receipt whose first attribute 12 is missing or does not parse, a JWS whose signedDate is missing or is not a representable instant) and request_date at the endpoint. This reverses 0.6, where that fallback was the system clock and an injected clock could not move it, so the dateless and unreadable-date cases now pin a clock (2025-01-01 unless the case is about the clock) and two endpoint cases pin that the clock does move the verdict. A case whose verdict or asserted fields could move with the clock pins one.

Expected. verifyReceipt and verifySignedData answer {"status":"ok","environment":E} or {"status":"error","reason":R}. On ok, environment is the environment the result states beside its payload, "Production", "Sandbox" or null, compared with ReceiptPayload.environment() or JsonPayload.environment() (in the module's answer, its top-level environment member): a receipt's comes from receipt_type (Production and ProductionVPP are Production, ProductionSandbox and ProductionVPPSandbox Sandbox, anything else null), a JWS's from the first of the top-level environment, data.environment and summary.environment that is present (Production and Sandbox map, anything else null), and null when none is (DECISIONS.md R42). Every ok case states it. fields maps a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) to a value, evaluated on the verified payload as JSON: ReceiptPayload.toJson() for receipts, JsonPayload.json() for JWS. One extension: a reference token written [key=value] selects the single element of an array whose member key is the JSON string value, and a runner fails the case unless exactly one element matches. lengths maps a pointer to the length of the array there. toJson, when present, is one valid output of toJson(): the runner parses it and the port's output as JSON and compares the parsed values (deep equality; numbers as numbers, strings as strings), never the bytes. Receipt JSON uses the design's keys: snake_case, dates as *_ms epoch milliseconds (numbers), 64-bit ids as strings, bytes as standard base64 with padding, unknown_attributes as {"<type>": ["<base64>", ...]} with values in receipt order. Owner rules of 2026-09-27 the receipt vectors pin: the first occurrence of a known attribute wins, for the typed field and for the chain date; every attribute that does not end up in a typed field (a later copy of a known attribute, or a known attribute whose value does not parse, whose typed field is then null) goes raw into unknown_attributes, the in-app ones into that purchase's unknown_attributes. A date attribute whose string is empty means not set: its typed field is null and it is not kept raw; an empty non-date string is the value "". A date decodes only in the exact form YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ (year 0000 to 9999, uppercase T and Z, a real calendar date, hours 00 to 23, minutes and seconds 00 to 59, no fraction, no offset); any other non-empty date string is null and kept raw, and an attribute 12 that does not decode leaves the chain instant to the clock. An IA5String holding a byte at or above 0x80, and an INTEGER that is not DER (empty or with a redundant leading octet), do not parse either: null and kept raw. verifyReceiptEndpoint always returns Apple's response body; expected.fields is evaluated on it and always pins /status, unless the case lists its outcomes (below). 0.7 exposes no failure reason beside the body, so the 0.6 failureReason is gone. Everywhere, null means absent or JSON null; numbers compare by value (1722945600000.0 equals 1722945600000) and integers exactly, so a runner parses without rounding (the endpoint's download_id is 2^63-1 as a JSON number). A field a case does not list is not pinned.

Failure messages. An error expectation may carry messageMustNotContain, a list of code points the failure message must not contain; the runner checks the message the port exposes. It pins that input quoted in a message (a JWS alg with CR, LF, NEL, U+2028 and a bidi override) is neutralised before a caller logs it.

Listed outcomes. expected {"oneOf":[...]} lists every outcome a port may give: "ok" (the call verified; no field is checked) or a reason. The port's outcome must be one of them. INTERNAL_ERROR is never listed and no exception or panic may escape the call, so both always fail; a case with maxMillis must also finish within it. It is used where the outcome is port-defined (owner, 2026-09-27): encoding oddities inside certificates the chain uses, and signer quirks where ports read the envelope differently (docs/design/0.7-api.md, Reading certificates and signed attributes). At the endpoint, whose call answers a body rather than a verdict, oneOf lists the /status values a port may answer and no other field is pinned. A case that lists "ok", or status 0, is tagged tolerant.

JSON reading. A JSON object with a duplicate member keeps the last one, in a JWS header, a JWS payload and an endpoint body; receipt attributes are the other way round (the first occurrence wins). A JWS header must be strict UTF-8 with no byte-order mark, and only whitespace may follow the header or payload object: trailing content after the header is MALFORMED, after the payload it is carried past the signature and is UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD when the signature verifies (lead, 2026-09-27). A runner parses what a port returns the same strict way, so a port that appended content to its output would fail.

Time budget. A case may carry maxMillis, a wall-clock budget for the verify call. The runner measures the call after one warm-up call of the same case and fails if it exceeds the budget. It is set on the denial-of-service cases (tag dos), which pin that a certificate no pinned root vouches for is rejected, or ignored, without its key being parsed or used, and on the tolerant cases. The figure is 2000, one for every port: an honest verify never touches the untrusted key and finishes in a few milliseconds even on a slow CI box, while an implementation that decodes or verifies with the oversized key first spends seconds (a single 262144-bit modexp is about 5 s in Go; a 65536-bit key is expensive in every measured library). Timing is a coarse backstop; each port also asserts directly, in its own runner, that no verification used the stranger key.

Reasons. The 0.7 set: MALFORMED, TOO_LARGE, INVALID_SIGNATURE, UNTRUSTED_CHAIN, INVALID_CERTIFICATE, INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD, INTERNAL_ERROR. Carried per the design's mapping: INVALID_CHAIN is UNTRUSTED_CHAIN; INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT, INVALID_JWS_FORMAT and MALFORMED_REQUEST fold into MALFORMED; REQUEST_TOO_LARGE is TOO_LARGE. Where the design is more specific the specific rule wins: a certificate outside its validity window at the chain instant is INVALID_CERTIFICATE (owner, 2026-09-27; tag validity-window); every input over a size cap is TOO_LARGE (the Bounds table); and a JWS payload that is not a JSON object is carried past the signature (the parse-before-signature rule), so the two unsigned 0.6 payload cases are INVALID_SIGNATURE and their signed twins UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD. None of the twelve 0.6 INTERNAL_ERROR cases stays INTERNAL_ERROR: four receipts whose Apple-signed content does not parse as an attribute set are UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD; the unreadable creation date and the unparseable in-app purchase verify with their raw octets in unknown_attributes; the six JWS claim-type cases verify because 0.7 returns the payload untyped. No input can make a correct library answer INTERNAL_ERROR, so no case expects it.

Fixtures. The registry works as in the 0.6 file: codec and contentSha256 over the decoded logical bytes, re-hashed by every runner. 0.7 checks Apple's WWDR marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1 on the receipt intermediate, which no 0.6 synthetic receipt chain carried, so every generated receipt was re-minted for this file into fixtures/generated-0.7/ by the same generators with TestPki stamping the marker (fresh keys; same payloads), VerifierApiFixtures writes the inputs new in 0.7 (including the three base64 strings at and over the receipt cap), and HardeningParityFixtures writes the denial-of-service and signer-algorithm inputs of the hardening parity work. receipt-der-trailing-byte.der there is receipt.der plus one zero byte, written by node tools/generate-limit-fixtures.mjs. The directory sits beside fixtures/generated/, which keeps the JWS fixtures and the 0.6 receipts that port unit tests, fuzz harnesses and smoke programs still read. JWS fixtures, public receipts, Apple's files, the request-body limits and the one over-cap receipt string refused for size before anything is decoded are the 0.6 files, unchanged. Regenerate with: mvn -B -q -f java/pom.xml test-compile; mvn -B -q -f java/pom.xml dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=/tmp/cp.txt; then java -cp "java/target/test-classes:java/target/classes:$(cat /tmp/cp.txt)" io.github.emindeniz99.applepurchasereceiptverifier.<Generator> <dir>/generated for PortDivergenceFixtures, HostileReceiptFixtures, AbsentSignerFixture, ReceiptCmsDefectFixtures, ReceiptIdsFixture and VerificationOrderFixtures, and mvn -B -q -f java/pom.xml surefire:test -Dtest=FixtureGeneratorTest -Dfixtures.generate=true -Daprv.fixtures.dir=<dir>; copy the receipt files and their roots into fixtures/generated-0.7/ and re-hash. LargeReceiptFixture and VerifierApiFixtures take fixtures/generated-0.7 and ReceiptBase64CapFixture takes fixtures, each its default when given no argument, and node tools/generate-limit-fixtures.mjs runs after ReceiptBase64CapFixture. None of the three is pointed at a generated/ directory: their outputs run to megabytes, and only generated-0.7/ and limits/ may hold a fixture over 100 KB. ReviewParityFixtures (review-*), OwnerDecisionFixtures (owner-*), IntermediateKeyUsageFixtures (keyusage-*), CertificateDerFixtures (der-*) and ExpiredMarkerFixtures (expired-marker-*) write straight into fixtures/generated-0.7/, after the generators above, because each derives a few inputs from files already there. Asn1DepthFixtures (depth-*) also writes straight into fixtures/generated-0.7/, under its own root, so the ASN.1 depth inputs regenerate without re-keying anything else. SignedAttrsTypeFixtures (signed-attrs-*) does the same for the signedAttrs attribute whose type is not an OID. EnvironmentFixtures (environment-*) writes straight into fixtures/generated-0.7/ under its own root too: the JWS whose environment is at each of the three places, and one whose first place names neither.

toJson by value. toJson() must be valid UTF-8 JSON with the same value as the expected string; whitespace, key order and escaping style are free, so each port uses its language's standard JSON encoder (owner, 2026-09-27). The expected strings happen to be in the design's key order with JSON.stringify escaping, which a port need not match. Every key is present, a missing field is null, bytes are padded standard base64, 64-bit ids are decimal strings, booleans are booleans, and there is no NaN or Infinity. Values are pinned for the shared receipt, the ids receipt, the web-order-zero receipt, a non-ASCII product id, two escapes product ids and the genuine public receipts that verify.

"fault" names the one intentional defect of a negative case. It is documentation, not an assertion. Tags are free-form; owner-review marks a case whose expectation follows from an owner rule but deserves a second look.

cases.description: The shared generated StoreKit 2 transaction JWS verifies against its own pinned root and decodes to the manifested claims.

The input of the 0.6 wrong-bundle-id case, which a verifier configured for another app refused. 0.7 takes no bundle id: the JWS verifies and the payload carries the bundleId claim for the caller to compare.

The input of the 0.6 case that a Production-only accept set refused. 0.7 takes no environment: the Sandbox transaction verifies, the verifier states its environment (Sandbox) beside the payload, and the caller judges it itself.
The generated test chain does not verify against the default pinned Apple roots: anchor pinning, not system trust.

A JWS leaf lacking marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped alongside the fixture (PLAN.md 2.1 step 3). Not exercised by the Java suite today, which asserts the same fact against a run-time generated PKI instead.
A JWS intermediate lacking WWDR marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1 is rejected against its own pinned root. Not exercised by the Java suite today.
Chain validity is judged at the payload signedDate, not at verification time: a 2020-06-01 payload signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4).

The expired chain (valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01) signing a 2024-08-06 payload: the signedDate falls outside the certificates' validity window, which is INVALID_CERTIFICATE (owner, 2026-09-27: the Reason definition wins over the 0.6 INVALID_CHAIN mapping). Deterministic: the window is fixed and in the past.
Apple's own app-store-server-library mock transactionInfo verifies against Apple's vendored test CA; cross-library parity on the exact upstream bytes.

Apple's wrongBundleId mock, which 0.6 refused on the bundle-id claim. It is a genuine TEST notification under Apple's test CA, so it verifies, and the payload shows the other app's bundle id at data.bundleId for the caller to judge.
Apple's missingX5CHeaderClaim mock fixture is rejected at header parsing: no x5c means no chain to validate (PLAN.md 2.1 step 2).
An Xcode/StoreKit-Test signed transaction carries a single self-signed certificate in x5c; requiring exactly three certificates rejects it before any chain work.
The shared generated Sandbox AppTransaction verifies and the payload carries the manifested claims unchanged.
The shared generated Production AppTransaction verifies and the payload carries receiptType "Production" and its appAppleId unchanged.

The input of the 0.6 case that a verifier bound to appAppleId 999 refused. 0.7 takes no appAppleId: the Production AppTransaction verifies and the payload shows appAppleId 123456789 for the caller to compare.
verifySignedData checks the chain and the signature and judges no claim: the shared transaction verifies and its claims come back unchanged.
Apple's mock renewalInfo carries no bundleId claim; verifySignedData needs none, and the chain and signature hold against Apple's test CA.
Apple's mock App Store Server Notification V2 payload verifies through verifySignedData against Apple's test CA.
An Xcode/StoreKit-Test signed renewal info carries a single self-signed certificate in x5c. Requiring exactly three certificates refuses it before any chain work.

The shared generated receipt verifies and every modelled attribute decodes to the manifested value. Its sha1_hash is SHA-1 over device id 112233445566778899aabbccddeeff00, opaque_value and bundle_id_bytes, the three raw fields the README's device-hash example hashes. Pins the toJson value too.

The input of the 0.6 case that refused device id 102233445566778899aabbccddeeff00 as DEVICE_HASH_MISMATCH. 0.7 takes no device id: the receipt verifies and returns opaque_value, sha1_hash and bundle_id_bytes raw, so the caller computes SHA-1(device id || opaque_value || bundle_id_bytes) and compares it with sha1_hash. For that device id the comparison fails; for 112233445566778899aabbccddeeff00 it holds.
The input of the 0.6 case that a verifier configured for another app refused. 0.7 takes no bundle id: the receipt verifies and shows bundle_id (and its raw octets) for the caller to compare.
A byte-identical payload signed by a second, independently generated receipt PKI is rejected against the first PKI root.
Xcode-style receipts wrap the attribute SET in an extra OCTET STRING; parsers must unwrap it rather than reject the receipt.

A signer leaf lacking OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped with the fixture (PLAN.md D13; closes the developer-certificate forgery hole).
Receipt chain validity is judged at the receipt creation date (attribute 12): a 2020-06-01 receipt signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.2 step 2).
The expired receipt chain (valid 2020 to 2021) signing a 2024-08-06 receipt: the creation date falls outside the certificates' validity window: INVALID_CERTIFICATE (owner, 2026-09-27).
Attribute types the library does not model are surfaced raw rather than dropped (PLAN.md D10): the shared receipt carries type 9999 with value bytes 01 02 03.

A genuine Apple-signed sandbox receipt on the newer G5 signing chain verifies against the default pinned Apple roots. Pins the toJson value: unmodelled values stay raw. Apple writes attribute 1712 as an empty IA5String; an empty date means not set, so cancellation_date_ms is null and no "1712" key appears (lead, 2026-09-27). receipt/in-app-unparseable-fields-are-kept-raw pins the other side: a non-empty date that does not parse is kept raw.
A genuine legacy receipt with a full SHA-1 signing chain and 187 in-app purchases verifies against the default pinned Apple roots. Pins the toJson value.
An Xcode-signed receipt carrying real purchases does not verify against the default Apple roots: its locally signed chain reaches no pinned root.

A genuine Xcode-generated app receipt from Apple's own test data is rejected against the real Apple roots. Chain validation runs before the signer-purpose check, so the reason is UNTRUSTED_CHAIN and not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (PLAN.md 2.2 step 3).

The endpoint answers status 0 for a sandbox receipt on the SANDBOX environment, rendering numbers as strings and dates as Apple's three-field triple. request_date follows the config clock and is left unasserted here; endpoint/request-date-is-the-verification-clock pins it.

request_date comes from the config clock. The receipt states its creation date, so the clock does not move the chain instant or receipt_creation_date. The three renderings are Apple's triple: Etc/GMT text, epoch milliseconds as a string, and America/Los_Angeles.
A sandbox receipt presented to a production instance routes to 21007 and the response carries neither receipt nor environment.
A receipt that does not chain to the endpoint trust anchors answers 21003 (could not be authenticated), never 21002.
receipt_type "Production" on a production instance answers 0.
receipt_type "Production" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" counts as production (PLAN.md D10 fail-closed routing set).
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" is a sandbox type despite the prefix; on a production instance it answers 21007. The misroute this case pins was found by adversarial review.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" on a sandbox instance answers 0.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox (fail closed), so a production instance answers 21007.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox and answers 0 there.

A receipt attribute whose type INTEGER is 2^31, one past the largest signed 32-bit value. The receipt is sound in every other way: trusted chain, WWDR and receipt-signing markers, valid signature, correct bundle id. The type cannot be represented (unknown_attributes is keyed by a 32-bit type), so the payload does not parse. The walk that looks for the creation date fails with it, so the chain is judged at the config clock (pinned inside the 2024 to 2050 window). Apple signed content the library cannot read: UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD. Renaming or clamping the type would let two ports disagree about what the same bytes contain.

The same over-range attribute type at the endpoint answers 21009 (UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD), not 21002 and not 21003: the receipt authenticates, and it is signed content the library cannot represent. 21002 would tell an app server the client sent a malformed receipt.

A receipt carrying no attribute 12 verifies with receipt_creation_date_ms null: the creation date is optional, and with none to anchor on, certificate validity is judged at the config clock, pinned to 2025-01-01 inside the 2024 to 2050 window. The two endpoint clock cases pin that the clock really is that instant.

The dateless receipt under a chain valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01, with the clock pinned to 2020-06-01. In 0.6 the clock only stamped request_date and this answered 21003. In 0.7 the config clock is also the chain instant for a receipt that states no creation date, so the chain is valid at it and the answer is 0.

The other direction: the dateless receipt under a chain valid until 2050, with the clock pinned to 2099. The config clock is the chain instant for a receipt that states no creation date, the chain has expired at it, and the answer is 21003 (0.6 answered 0 here).

A payload carrying no signedDate, signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01. With no date of its own, certificate validity is judged at the config clock, pinned to 2025-01-01, where the chain has expired: INVALID_CERTIFICATE. A port that skipped the validity check for a dateless payload would accept it.

A payload that states no signing time still verifies, and the payload shows no signedDate. Certificate validity is judged at the config clock, pinned to 2025-01-01, where this chain (valid 2024 to 2050) is live. The mirror of transaction/reject-dateless-payload-under-an-expired-chain.

One character of the payload segment was rewritten after the JWS was signed, so the ES256 signature no longer covers the bytes served. The header, the three x5c entries, both marker OIDs, the chain at the payload's own signedDate and the payload JSON are all intact, so INVALID_SIGNATURE is the first verdict reachable.

The first x5c entry is base64 of the ASCII text "not a certificate"; well-formed base64 that decodes to bytes no X.509 parser can read. The header was signed in that state, so the signature genuinely covers what is served and the unparseable leaf is the only defect. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE rather than MALFORMED (the entry is present, is a string, and the array still holds exactly three) and rather than INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (nothing was parsed, so no marker OID could be looked for). The entry chosen is x5c[0] on purpose: Java parses the third entry and the other eight ports never touch it, so a vector built on x5c[2] would pin a divergence instead of a shared rule.

One byte of the receipt's signed payload was flipped after signing, so the CMS content digest no longer matches the one the signature covers. The byte belongs to attribute 9999, which is not modelled, so the creation date still reads, the chain still builds at it and both marker OIDs are present. The signature check is the only thing left to fail.

A second point on the attribute-type ceiling: type 2^32 + 2, which truncated to 32 bits becomes 2, the bundle id attribute, carrying a well-formed UTF8String reading "com.attacker.app". A port that wrapped instead of refusing would read a second bundle id. The receipt is otherwise sound, so the answer is UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD for the same reason as at 2^31; the chain is judged at the config clock because the walk for the creation date fails.

Four non-base64url characters are appended to the signature segment of an otherwise genuine, verifying transaction. Everything before the segment decode is intact, so the only question this pins is whether a port decodes a compact-JWS segment strictly. A lenient decoder drops the characters it does not recognise and recovers the original 64 signature bytes, so the payload verifies and the port answers ok; a strict one refuses the segment. This is pinned strict: RFC 7515 section 2 defines the segments as unpadded base64url, and accepting anything else means a port accepts bytes the signature does not cover.

The signature segment of a genuine, verifying transaction is padded to a multiple of four with '='. RFC 7515 section 2 specifies base64url with the padding omitted, so the padded spelling is not a compact JWS. As with the trailing-junk case the decoded signature bytes are unchanged, so a port that tolerates padding answers ok and a port that does not refuses the segment.

The final character of the signature segment is replaced by one that decodes to the same bytes with a different bit pattern in the trailing bits base64url does not use. The decoded signature is byte-identical to the genuine one, so the ES256 check passes wherever the segment decodes at all: this is the same signed transaction under a second spelling. That is what makes it the sharpest of the three. A caller that deduplicates on the JWS string rather than on transactionId (PLAN.md D4) gets a fresh cache key for a payload it has already honoured, so the lenient answer is an accept for every one of the sixteen spellings this substitution admits.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: canonical standard base64, one line: what base64EncodedString(options: []) emits. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: a trailing line feed after the padding. Apple's verifyReceipt answered 21002 to this spelling of genuine receipts, production and sandbox, on 2026-09-23 (docs/evidence/2026-09-23-verifyreceipt-base64.md), so it is MALFORMED: receipt-data is standard-alphabet base64 with the canonical padding and nothing else. Same DER underneath as receipt-base64/accept-genuine, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine receipt's base64 with its final data character removed and three '=' appended: the data length is 1 mod 4, which no base64 encoding can have, yet the total is a multiple of four. The unpadded data length must be checked first, and three '=' is never canonical.

The header is `{"alg":"ES256","x5c":[1,2,3]}` and was signed in that state, so the ES256 signature covers exactly the bytes served and the JSON types are the only defect. The array is present and holds exactly three entries, so what fails is the type of each one, before any of them is base64-decoded: MALFORMED, the same verdict a header with no x5c at all gets, and not INVALID_CERTIFICATE, which would say something was decoded and found wanting. The statically typed ports get this from decoding the header into an array of strings; the dynamically typed ones have to check it, and Python did not until fuzzing walked a TypeError out of base64.b64decode and past every `except` in the library. A genuinely signed payload whose signedDate is 1e300, a number that is no representable instant. Such a signedDate does not parse (owner, 2026-09-27), so the config clock, pinned to 2025-01-01 inside the chain's 2024 to 2050 window, stands in for the chain check and the JWS verifies, its payload unchanged. 0.6 judged the chain at the impossible instant and answered INVALID_CHAIN.

One byte of x5c[1] is changed: the basicConstraints extnValue OCTET STRING is left claiming 127 content bytes inside an extension that declares 15, so the certificate stops decoding partway through its extension block. Everything before that region is intact and the header was signed in this state. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE; the entry is present, is a string and decodes from base64, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. What this vector pins that `transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate` cannot is that a port must PARSE an x5c certificate rather than scan it: the corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1" accepts the whole JWS. It is x5c[1] rather than x5c[0] so that the two certificate vectors cover both entries every port loads.

x5c[1]'s namedCurve is rewritten to 1.2.840.10045.3.1.10, which is unassigned, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so the certificate is genuine in every other respect and a broken issuer signature is not what a port objects to first. A public key cannot be built on a curve the implementation does not have, so the certificate is one this library never understood: INVALID_CERTIFICATE, alongside the other two x5c defects, rather than UNTRUSTED_CHAIN. That reading was adopted AGAINST the six-to-three majority the ports arrived with, because the three in the minority (java, swift, go) reject the certificate while decoding it and pinning UNTRUSTED_CHAIN would have required them to defer a rejection they already make. It also closes a latent escape in Node, where reading the certificate's public key raises a raw OpenSSL decode error and only the order of the issuer check kept it from reaching a caller. The requirement underneath the reason is that the failure is a verdict at all: an unimplemented curve surfaces as a library-specific exception type; cryptography's UnsupportedAlgorithm was not in Python's except list; and a caller catching the verification error sees a crash instead.

x5c[1] claims X.509 version 11, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so nothing else about it is wrong: the extensions decode, the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, and it really did issue the leaf. X.509 defines v1, v2 and v3 and nothing else, so the only thing that can reject this input is a version check, which is why a port without one accepts a certificate whose format it does not know. INVALID_CERTIFICATE: the bytes are not a certificate this library can be said to have understood, and the fault is in the certificate rather than in the path it sits on.

x5c[0] carries its basicConstraints extension twice; a byte-identical second copy appended to the extension list; and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate so the certificate is genuine in every other respect: the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, the key is the one that signed the JWS, and the intermediate really did issue it. RFC 5280 4.2 says a certificate MUST NOT include more than one instance of a particular extension, and a parser that allows one has to pick a copy, so two ports reading the same bytes can disagree about whether the certificate is a CA, what it may be used for, or whether it carries a marker OID at all. Port-defined (owner, 2026-10-05): BouncyCastle refuses the certificate at parse ("repeated extension found"), so Java answers INVALID_CERTIFICATE; OpenSSL parses it, marks its extensions invalid because basicConstraints repeats (EXFLAG_INVALID, crypto/x509/v3_purp.c) and then takes no certificate as its issuer, so the core answers UNTRUSTED_CHAIN. Both refuse, and neither as INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, which would say the extensions were read and the marker OID was missing. The duplicated extension is basicConstraints rather than the marker OID because it is the one every port reaches: a port that scans for 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 and never decodes the rest of the block accepts this JWS. It sits on the leaf because that is the certificate whose extensions every port touches first, and Python's fuzzer found it there; cryptography raises DuplicateExtension, which derives from Exception rather than ValueError and so passed every except in the JWS path and reached the caller as a crash. DECISIONS.md R20.

The THIRD x5c entry is base64 of the ASCII text "not a certificate"; well-formed base64 that decodes to bytes no X.509 parser can read, and the header was signed in that state, so the unparseable third entry is the only defect. It is the index twin of transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate, which deliberately sits on x5c[0] because this index was the one differential no shared vector covered: java decoded and parsed all three entries and answered INVALID_CERTIFICATE, while node, python, swift, go, ruby, rust, php and dotnet never touched the third entry and VERIFIED the JWS. Eight ports to one, and the majority was overruled by the rule that settled transaction/reject-x5c-unimplemented-curve: pinning acceptance would have made java drop a rejection it already makes, and no reading of this library lets an input it cannot parse through because the parse was optional. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, the same verdict the other two unreadable-certificate vectors carry. What does NOT change is trust: x5c[2] is still never compared to an anchor and never trusted anywhere, so a well-formed JWS whose third entry an attacker swapped still verifies or fails exactly as before; the entry now has to be a certificate, not the right one.

One exclamation mark is inserted in the middle of x5c[0]. Before this vector node, python, swift, ruby, rust and php skipped it and verified the JWS; java, go and dotnet refused it. x5c[0] is the genuine leaf, re-spelled; x5c[1], x5c[2], the payload and the DER underneath are untouched, and the header was signed in this state, so the ES256 signature covers exactly the bytes served and the spelling is the only defect. RFC 7515 section 4.1.6 makes each x5c entry base64 (RFC 4648 section 4, NOT base64url) of a DER certificate, and RFC 4648 section 3.3 has a decoder reject characters outside the alphabet unless the referring specification says otherwise, which RFC 7515 does not. A decoder that skips or translates what it does not expect recovers the genuine leaf and VERIFIES the JWS, so INVALID_CERTIFICATE here can only come from the x5c decode; it is the verdict an x5c entry that does not decode to a certificate already gets (transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate).

x5c[0] is spelled in the base64url alphabet: every + is - and every / is _, and no standard-only character is left, so a decoder that refuses only a MIXED alphabet still accepts it. x5c[0] is the genuine leaf with its '=' padding omitted. RFC 4648 section 3.2 requires the padding unless the referring specification says otherwise, and RFC 7515 section 4.1.6 does not (it is base64url segments, not x5c entries, that drop it), so this is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, the rule receipt-data follows too: standard alphabet, canonical padding, nothing else. x5c[0] is the genuine leaf with one '=' more than its length calls for. No encoder emits it, and a decoder that stops at the first '=' or skips surplus padding (Swift's Data(base64Encoded:) on Linux) reads it as the genuine certificate and verifies the JWS. The payload's signedDate is written 1722945600000.0, the same instant as every other generated transaction, spelled with a decimal point. JSON draws no line between that and 1722945600000, so the claim is the same and the JWS verifies; the payload comes back unchanged and the runner compares the number by value. The certificate a legacy PKCS#7 receipt is signed by claims X.509 version 11, and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate so nothing else about it is wrong. The receipt is genuine in every other respect; the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date; so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. X.509 defines v1, v2 and v3 and nothing else, so only a version check can reject this input. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, the reason transaction/reject-x5c-certificate-version-11 pins for the same mutation in a JWS header. It needs its own vector because the version check sat on the JWS path alone in node, python, ruby and dotnet: the four ports that settle what their platform decoder lets past while the verdict is still "this is not a certificate" were settling it for x5c entries only, and the CMS signer went unchecked. Either INVALID_CERTIFICATE or MALFORMED is accepted: a port that decodes the unsigned certificate bag as a whole refuses this entry as a malformed bag before it reaches the signer (lead, 2026-09-27).

The signer certificate carries its basicConstraints extension twice; a byte-identical second copy appended to the extension list; and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate. The receipt is genuine in every other respect; the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date; so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. RFC 5280 4.2 forbids a second instance of any extension, and a reader that allows one has to pick which copy the certificate means, so the same bytes stop having one answer to "is this a CA", "what may it be used for" and "does it carry the receipt-signing marker OID"; the last of which this path asks. Not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, which would say the extensions were read and the marker OID was missing. The duplicated extension is basicConstraints rather than the marker OID for the same reason as in the JWS twin: it is the one a port reaches even if it only scans for 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1. Port-defined: BouncyCastle refuses the certificate while it reads the unsigned certificate bag ("repeated extension found"), so Java answers MALFORMED for the bag (lead, 2026-09-27); OpenSSL parses it, marks its extensions invalid because basicConstraints repeats (EXFLAG_INVALID, crypto/x509/v3_purp.c) and then takes no certificate as its issuer, so the core answers UNTRUSTED_CHAIN (owner, 2026-10-05). The core answered INVALID_CERTIFICATE from a reader of its own until then, which the list keeps. DECISIONS.md R20.

The signer's KEY is the mutation. The receipt is signed with a real P-256 key, and the certificate that key sits in then names 1.2.840.10045.3.1.10, which is unassigned, with the TBS re-signed by the intermediate. The receipt is genuine in every other respect; the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date; so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. A public key cannot be built on a curve the implementation does not have, so the signature this receipt carries can never be checked; and the port must say so as a verdict about the certificate, before it reaches the signature at all. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, as transaction/reject-x5c-unimplemented-curve pins, and specifically NOT the verdict a port reaches by noticing that the key is not RSA: a readable non-RSA signer key is a different input with a different answer, and this one is a certificate the library never understood. The requirement underneath the reason is that the failure is a verdict at all; an unimplemented curve surfaces as a library-specific exception type, and a caller catching the verification error otherwise sees a crash.

One byte of the signer certificate is changed, and it is one byte further in than the JWS twin changes. transaction/reject-x5c-corrupt-extension rewrites the extnValue OCTET STRING's own length, which breaks the DER of everything that contains it; harmless in a JWS header, where the certificate is a base64 string of its own, and wrong inside a CMS, where it would break the receipt's DER and make every port that walks the whole blob answer about the receipt instead of about the certificate. So the corruption sits INSIDE the OCTET STRING: the BasicConstraints SEQUENCE it holds is left claiming 127 content bytes in a two-byte value. A reader walking generic ASN.1 sees a well-formed primitive of the length it declares and never looks in, so the receipt parses, the chain validates, the payload is intact and the CMS signature is real; only a reader that DECODES the signer's extension block finds the defect, and that is precisely what this vector observes. The certificate has no TBS left to re-sign and no verifier can reach its signature to notice. The signer is embedded and is the certificate the SignerInfo names, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. The corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1" accepts the whole receipt. Port-defined: Java refuses the certificate while it reads the unsigned certificate bag, so it answers MALFORMED for the bag (lead, 2026-09-27); OpenSSL parses it, marks its extensions invalid because basicConstraints does not decode (EXFLAG_INVALID, crypto/x509/v3_purp.c) and then takes no certificate as its issuer, so the core answers UNTRUSTED_CHAIN (owner, 2026-10-05). The core answered INVALID_CERTIFICATE from a reader of its own until then, which the list keeps. DECISIONS.md R20.

The SignerInfo names an issuer and serial no embedded entry carries, and the bag also holds one entry that is not a certificate. The signer is simply not embedded, which is MALFORMED; the malformed stranger is unrelated to the SignerInfo and must not turn that into INVALID_CERTIFICATE. A port has to match the SignerInfo against each entry's raw identity before it judges any entry.

The whole input is `..`; two dots and nothing else. It splits into exactly three segments, so a port that counts them and stops gets past that check with no header to read, and every later step is then working from nothing. MALFORMED. This is the shortest input in the vector set and the one java's fuzzing walked out of the library as a NullPointerException rather than a verdict: Jackson's readTree returns null for zero bytes, and the next line asks that null for `alg`. What the vector requires is what every negative vector requires; that the answer is a verdict a caller can catch on the error type it was told to catch.

The header segment is empty and the payload and signature are the genuine ones from a real JWS over the fixture root, so the empty header is the only defect. An empty segment is valid base64url of zero bytes, and zero bytes are not a JSON object; the distinction that matters, because a decoder that answers \"nothing\" instead of raising hands the caller a null the next line dereferences. MALFORMED, the same verdict a header that is not base64url JSON gets, and reached before any certificate is decoded.

The genuine header and signature around an empty payload segment. An empty segment is valid base64url of zero bytes, so the compact structure is whole and this is content that does not parse: per the 0.7 parse-before-signature rule it is carried past the chain (judged at the config clock) and the signature, which covers the original payload and fails: INVALID_SIGNATURE. signed-data/unreadable-empty-payload is the same shape genuinely signed.

The header segment is valid base64url of `[\"ES256\",[]]`; valid JSON, and not an object. RFC 7515 7.1 makes the JOSE header a JSON object; an array has no member to read `alg` or `x5c` from, and a port that indexes into it by name has to decide that on purpose rather than discover it by accident. The array's contents are chosen to look like the two things a header carries, so a port that pattern-matches rather than reads members cannot pass by luck. MALFORMED.

The header segment decodes to `42`. RFC 8259 2 makes a bare scalar a complete JSON text, so a port that asks only \"does this parse as JSON\" accepts it and then reads `alg` off a number. It is the second of the two non-object shapes a JSON document can take, and it is here beside the array because the ports' JSON readers fail differently on the two: a statically typed decode into a map refuses both, a dynamically typed one refuses neither until something checks. MALFORMED.

The genuine header and signature around a payload that is the JSON array [1,2,3]. The payload is not a JSON object, so per the 0.7 parse-before-signature rule it is carried past the chain (judged at the config clock) and the signature, which covers the original payload and fails: INVALID_SIGNATURE. signed-data/unreadable-json-array-payload is the same shape genuinely signed.

The byte half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of about 1 MiB of DER (1,034,699 bytes, the 0.6 receipt plus the WWDR marker on its intermediate), which every port MUST accept. Its payload holds 9,237 ASN.1 nodes, under half the node budget, so accepting it says something about bytes alone. 2,300 in-app purchases with product ids padded to 262 characters; the first and last keep short ids so the case can select them.

The node half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt whose payload is one parse of 19,897 nodes (99.5% of the 20,000 the contract promises), which every port MUST accept. Ten in-app purchases plus 4,955 three-byte attributes of unmodelled types; the fields pin one at each end of the run so a port cannot pass by skipping what it does not recognise.

App-level attributes 1 (app item id), 15 (download id) and 16 (version external identifier) and in-app 1713 (is trial period) are decoded, not left in unknown_attributes. The ids are JSON strings in toJson because the download id here is 2^63-1, far above 2^53, and 1713 appears on both sides of the boolean. Pins the toJson value too.

A receipt carrying none of attributes 1, 15, 16 or 1713 reports them as null rather than 0 or empty. Absent and present-but-zero are different answers: Apple's sandbox sends 0 for the three ids when it carries them.

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint echoes the four decoded attributes under Apple's own keys and in Apple's own JSON types. Attribute 1 appears TWICE, as adam_id and as app_item_id, because Apple's response reference defines adam_id as "See app_item_id" and both carry the same value. The three app-level ids are JSON numbers, unlike the in-app integers, which Apple renders as strings; download_id is 2^53+1, so a port serialising through a double answers 9007199254740992 and fails. Attribute 1713 becomes is_trial_period, the string "true" or "false", exactly as 1719 becomes is_in_intro_offer_period. This case pins no clock, so request_date* is left unasserted.

An attribute the receipt does not carry leaves its key OUT of the endpoint's answer rather than emitting JSON null: the shared sandbox receipt carries none of the four, so adam_id, app_item_id, download_id, version_external_identifier and a purchase's is_trial_period are all absent. That is what Apple does, and it is what the existing optional keys already do here.

A genuine sandbox receipt carries attribute types 1, 15 and 16 with value 0, and 1713 with value 0 on every in-app entry, which is what Apple's verifyReceipt echoes as adam_id, app_item_id, download_id, version_external_identifier and is_trial_period for a sandbox receipt. Present-with-zero is a decoded 0, not absent: receipt/ids-absent-when-not-carried pins the other case.

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint renders the zero-valued ids a genuine sandbox receipt carries exactly as Apple does for a sandbox receipt: adam_id, app_item_id, download_id and version_external_identifier as the JSON number 0, and is_trial_period as the string "false".

The device-hash inputs pinned on Apple-signed bytes: for the genuine sandbox receipt vendored here, the published device id 956328d9cc6a47f4be406953fb0ab6c7 makes SHA-1(device id || opaque_value || bundle_id_bytes) equal sha1_hash byte for byte. The library does not hash; the case pins the three raw fields the README example hashes, so a port that re-encoded bundle_id_bytes or trimmed opaque_value is caught on genuine bytes.

The input of the 0.6 case that refused a device id one bit away from the genuine one as DEVICE_HASH_MISMATCH. 0.7 takes no device id: the receipt verifies and returns the three raw fields, and the caller's own SHA-1 over device id 856328d9cc6a47f4be406953fb0ab6c7 fails to match sha1_hash.

The input of the 0.6 case that refused a configured "com.Example.app" because attribute 2 is compared byte for byte. 0.7 compares nothing: the receipt verifies and returns bundle_id and its raw octets, and a caller comparing "com.Example.app" must compare exactly, as the README checklist says.

The certificate sitting where the intermediate belongs is a receipt-signing end entity, and the signer really was issued by it. Every signature and every name link in the path is genuine, every validity window covers the receipt's creation date, and the path terminates at the pinned root; the only defect is that basicConstraints says that certificate may not issue. A port that chains on issuer names and signatures alone accepts it, which would let any receipt-signing leaf mint signers of its own.

A genuine signer under a genuine intermediate, with the intermediate left out of the CMS certificate bag, so no path reaches the pinned root. Paired with receipt/reject-leaf-presented-as-intermediate it separates the two ways an issuer can be wrong: absent, and present but not a CA.

The SignerInfo's signature is an OCTET STRING of zero bytes. DER length-prefixes it, so an empty signature is well-formed ASN.1 and the receipt parses, the chain builds and the signer purpose checks out: the port has to reach the verification step and take a negative answer from it. A port that treats an empty signature as a parse failure, or that skips verification when there is nothing to verify, answers something else.

A CMS genuinely signed over zero bytes of encapsulated content. The envelope decodes, and the chain, both marker OIDs and the signature are genuine; the empty content is not an attribute set. Content inside a well-formed envelope that does not parse is carried past the signature (the chain judged at the config clock, since there is no creation date) and is UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD.

Attribute 12 is the IA5String "not-a-date". A date attribute that does not parse decodes to null and the clock stands in for it at the chain check (pinned to 2025-01-01, inside the 2024 to 2050 window). Nothing Apple signed is lost: attribute 12's raw value octets appear under unknown_attributes["12"] (owner, 2026-09-27). The receipt verifies; 0.6 answered INTERNAL_ERROR.

The same unreadable creation date, signed by a PKI with the same subject names that the verifier does not trust. The chain answers first: UNTRUSTED_CHAIN. An unreadable payload from an untrusted signer never surfaces as a format error.

The unreadable creation date under a chain valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01. The clock stands in for the date that does not parse, and at 2025-01-01 the certificates have expired: INVALID_CERTIFICATE. Proves the fallback instant is the clock rather than no validity check.

An in-app purchase (attribute 17) whose value is an OCTET STRING rather than an attribute SET. Attribute 17 is a known attribute whose value does not parse, so under the owner's 2026-09-27 rule it becomes no in_app entry and its raw octets go to unknown_attributes["17"]; the receipt verifies. 0.6 answered INTERNAL_ERROR, and the first 0.7 draft UNREADABLE_PAYLOAD. Flagged for review because it is the rule applied to the one composite attribute.

Attribute 12 twice, both 2020-06-01, under a chain valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01. The first occurrence wins for the typed field and for the chain date (owner, 2026-09-27), so the chain is judged inside its window and the receipt verifies; the second copy is kept raw under unknown_attributes["12"]. 0.6 treated two dates as none and judged at now. receipt/creation-date-twice-first-wins pins which copy is first.

A readable creation date beside a top-level entry that is not SEQUENCE { INTEGER, INTEGER, OCTET STRING }, under a chain valid 2020 to 2021. A verifying request body whose password field (accepted for wire compatibility and never read) holds U+00E9, a two-byte character, filling the body to exactly 3,145,728 UTF-8 bytes in 1,576,659 characters. A verifying request body carrying an ignored field of 63 nested arrays, so the body object and the arrays are 64 containers open at once: exactly the nesting limit. It verifies, status 0.

A raw request body whose receipt-data is the genuine sandbox receipt's canonical base64 (01-genuine) with U+FEFF in front of it, the mark written as its UTF-8 bytes rather than as a JSON escape. The input is the whole body, so the port's own parser is what reads it.

The first occurrence wins for the chain date and the typed field (owner, 2026-09-27), so the chain is judged inside its window and the receipt verifies with receipt_creation_date_ms 2020-06-01; the second copy is kept raw. A port that took the last date, or treated the pair as no date (the clock is pinned to 2025-01-01), answers INVALID_CERTIFICATE.

A purchase whose quantity (1701) is a UTF8String "1" rather than an INTEGER and whose purchase date (1704) is "not-a-date". Both typed fields are null, and both raw values appear under that purchase's unknown_attributes under their type numbers, so nothing Apple signed is lost (owner, 2026-09-27). The receipt verifies.

A product id holding a quote, a backslash, backspace, form feed, line feed, carriage return, tab, U+001F and U+2028. The expected toJson escapes them as JSON.stringify does; a port may escape differently, since the runner compares the parsed values.

A JWS whose x5c[1] is signed by no pinned root and carries a 262144-bit RSA modulus. A top-down chain check verifies x5c[1] against the pinned root, which fails, and never parses its key: UNTRUSTED_CHAIN, within maxMillis. A port that checks x5c[0] against x5c[1] first parses the oversized key and spends seconds (Go about 5 s per modexp).

A receipt whose signer names an intermediate that only eight untrusted certificates claim, each with a 65536-bit RSA modulus and none vouched for by the pinned root. A top-down check rejects them without parsing a key: UNTRUSTED_CHAIN, within maxMillis. A bottom-up builder verifies the signer against each oversized key and spends seconds.

A genuine receipt (signer, intermediate and root that verify) padded with seven stranger certificates named like the intermediate, each with a 65536-bit RSA modulus, ten certificates in all at the cap. The strangers are vouched for by no pinned root, so a top-down check ignores them (Q16) and the receipt verifies, within maxMillis. A bottom-up builder tries each stranger as the signer issuer and spends seconds before finding the real intermediate.

A receipt whose signer holds an ECDSA P-256 key and whose CMS signature is ECDSA with SHA-256, under the test PKI. The signer chains to a pinned root and carries the receipt-signing marker, so it verifies: 0.7 does not restrict the signer key or signature algorithm (owner Q15, change 3).
The ECDSA-signed receipt with one content byte flipped after signing: the ECDSA check fails, INVALID_SIGNATURE, so accepting any signer algorithm does not accept a bad signature.
A receipt signed with an RSA signer and a SHA-384 digest under the test PKI. Any digest the pinned chain signed is accepted (owner Q15), so it verifies.

A receipt whose CMS signature is RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 under the test PKI; the signature is genuine. Apple never signs receipts with RSA-PSS, so RSA-PSS support is port-defined (owner, 2026-09-27): the port may verify or refuse with one of the listed reasons, but must not crash and must finish within maxMillis. PHP refuses it, because its OpenSSL binding has no PSS mode and the owner rules out hand-written crypto.

The shared receipt with its first embedded certificate's outer signature, outside the signed TBS, written as a constructed BIT STRING of two primitive chunks, 03 01 00 and the raw signature octets. Port-defined (owner's orchestrator, 2026-09-29): OpenSSL joins the chunks' contents and then reads the first octet as the unused-bits count, so the core recovers the original signature and verifies; X.690 8.6.4 gives every segment its own unused-bits octet, so a BER-exact reader such as BouncyCastle sees 150 unused bits in the second chunk and answers MALFORMED. Apple's certificates are DER and never chunk a signature, so both readings are safe: the chain is judged either way and nothing unsigned is accepted. A port must answer one of the two, must not crash, and must finish within maxMillis. The X.690 spelling, with an unused-bits octet in each chunk, is the reverse (the core refuses it, Java verifies it) and is recorded in DECISIONS R20, not pinned here.

A summary notification (RENEWAL_EXTENSION, SUMMARY) carries neither a top-level environment nor data; its summary.environment, the third of the three places, is the result's environment (DECISIONS.md R42).

The first of the three places that is present decides, whatever it names: a top-level environment of Xcode makes the result's environment null although data.environment says Sandbox (DECISIONS.md R42).
